--- title: "Classification performance measures" description: "Presence can be scored on the calls at one threshold, on how well the probabilities rank the stations, or on whether the probabilities can be read as chances. Sensitivity, specificity and precision count misses and false alarms apart, ROC AUC scores the ranking at every threshold, and a calibration plot checks the probabilities." order: 4 categories: [validation, metrics, classification] --- {{< new-terms >}} ## Presence can be scored in three ways [Logistic regression](../03-supervised-learning/logistic-regression.qmd) scored its calls of present or absent by accuracy, and [Class imbalance](../06-assumptions-limitations/class-imbalance.qmd) showed that for a rare species accuracy hides the misses. Accuracy counts the calls at one threshold. But a model that predicts presence gives every station a probability, which also ranks the stations from most to least likely to hold the species. So there are three things to score: the calls, the ranking and the probabilities themselves. This page gives a common measure or check for each, and shows that a model can look much the same on one and clearly better on another. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Sensitivity, specificity and precision count misses and false alarms apart Accuracy adds up both kinds of right answer. Three measures keep them apart, each the share of one group of cases: - **Sensitivity**, also called recall: of the cases that are truly yes, the share called yes. Misses lower it. - **Specificity**: of the cases that are truly no, the share called no. False alarms lower it. - **Precision**: of the cases called yes, the share that are truly yes. False alarms lower it too, and when yes is rare they easily outnumber the true yeses: with 5 yeses in 100 cases, calling one no in ten yes gives about 10 false alarms. When nearly every case is no, accuracy is mostly specificity, so a model can miss most of the yeses and still look good. ::: {.diagram} ![The same twenty cases, four truly yes and sixteen truly no, with six called yes. Sensitivity is the share of true yeses called yes, lowered by misses. Specificity is the share of true noes called no, lowered by false alarms. Precision is the share of yes calls that are true, also lowered by false alarms.](img/three-measures.svg){fig-alt="Three cards show the same twenty cases in two rows: four truly yes, drawn filled, and sixteen truly no, drawn open. A dashed box marks the six the model called yes: three true yeses and three noes. One true yes lies outside the box. Sensitivity, lowered by misses: of the four true yeses, three were called yes and one, the miss, was not; 3 of 4. Specificity, lowered by false alarms: of the sixteen true noes, thirteen were called no and three, the false alarms, sit in the box; 13 of 16. Precision, lowered by false alarms: of the six yes calls, three are true and three are false alarms; 3 of 6. A note says accuracy, 16 of 20, hides the miss, because when yeses are few it mostly counts the noes."} ::: ## Measures at one threshold count the calls At a threshold, every station falls into one of four cells: true presences, false alarms, misses and true absences. Set out as a two-by-two table, they are called the **confusion matrix**, and every measure of the calls is worked out from it. One more measure is common: **balanced accuracy**, the average of sensitivity and specificity. It gives presence and absence equal weight, so a rule that calls every station present scores 0.5 however common the species is. ## ROC AUC scores the ranking at every threshold [Class imbalance](../06-assumptions-limitations/class-imbalance.qmd#upsampling-gives-the-same-answers-as-a-lower-threshold) drew the share of presences a model finds against the share of absences it calls present, at every threshold: its sensitivity against one minus its specificity. That curve is the **ROC curve** (receiver operating characteristic, a name from radar). The area under it, the **ROC AUC**, sums up the whole curve in one number, so models can be compared before a threshold is chosen. It is also the share of pairs, one station with the species and one without, in which the station with the species gets the higher probability. A ROC AUC of 1 ranks every station with the species above every station without it; 0.5 is no better than ranking at random. ## A calibration plot checks that probabilities can be read as chances A probability of presence is **calibrated** when it can be read as a chance: of the stations given 0.8, about 8 in 10 hold the species. ROC AUC cannot see this, because it depends only on the order of the probabilities: raising every probability, or squeezing them all towards 0.5, leaves the order and the ROC AUC unchanged. A **calibration plot** checks it directly. The log loss of [Loss functions](../04-how-algorithms-learn/loss-functions.qmd#counts-and-presence-have-their-own-losses) scores the probabilities in one number, but the plot shows where they go wrong. ## Worked example The outcome is `present`, whether the species was caught at a station at all. Three models predict it: - **Predicting the share present**: every station gets the share of the fitted stations with the species. It has no skill, and the other two should beat it. - **Logistic regression**, from [Logistic regression](../03-supervised-learning/logistic-regression.qmd), with each input entered as a straight line in the log-odds. - **Random forest**, from [Random forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd). For presence, each tree gives the share of stations with the species in the leaf a station falls in, and the forest averages those shares into a probability. As on [Regression performance measures](regression-metrics.qmd), every model is cross-validated on the same ten folds of sites, and each measure is worked out from the pooled out-of-fold probabilities. ### Preparing the data ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() set.seed(61) folds <- group_vfold_cv(survey, group = site_id, v = 10) inputs <- c("depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu", "substrate", "season", "longitude", "latitude") presence_recipe <- recipe(reformulate(inputs, "present"), data = survey) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |> step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) forest <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |> set_engine("ranger", seed = 1) |> set_mode("classification") models <- list( "Predicting the share present" = null_model(mode = "classification"), "Logistic regression" = logistic_reg(), "Random forest" = forest ) # every station's out-of-fold probability of presence, in the survey's order out_of_fold <- map(models, \(model) { fit_resamples(workflow(presence_recipe, model), folds, metrics = metric_set(roc_auc), control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE)) |> collect_predictions() |> arrange(.row) |> pull(.pred_yes) }) predictions <- as_tibble(out_of_fold) |> mutate(present = survey$present) |> pivot_longer(-present, names_to = "model", values_to = "probability") |> mutate(model = fct_inorder(model)) tibble(stations = nrow(survey), `share present` = mean(survey$present == "yes"), `outcome levels` = str_flatten(levels(survey$present), ", ")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| stations| share present|outcome levels | |--------:|-------------:|:--------------| | 800| 0.775|yes, no |
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression from sklearn.metrics import (accuracy_score, balanced_accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score, roc_auc_score) from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold, cross_val_predict from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() present = (survey["present"] == "yes").to_numpy() folds = GroupKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=61) inputs = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu", "substrate", "season", "longitude", "latitude"] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] numeric = [c for c in inputs if c not in categorical] def with_inputs(model): recipe = ColumnTransformer([ # scaling leaves an unpenalised fit unchanged and helps the solver ("numeric", Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("scale", StandardScaler())]), numeric), ("nominal", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", sparse_output=False), categorical), ]) return Pipeline([("recipe", recipe), ("model", model)]) models = { "Predicting the share present": DummyClassifier(strategy="prior"), "Logistic regression": LogisticRegression(C=np.inf, max_iter=5000), # as ranger does for probabilities: a few inputs at each question, # and no split of a leaf with fewer than 10 stations "Random forest": RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, max_features="sqrt", min_samples_split=10, random_state=1), } # every station's out-of-fold probability of presence, in the survey's order; # column 1 of predict_proba is the probability of True out_of_fold = {name: cross_val_predict(with_inputs(model), survey[inputs], present, cv=folds, groups=survey["site_id"], method="predict_proba")[:, 1] for name, model in models.items()} predictions = (pd.DataFrame(out_of_fold).assign(present=present) .melt(id_vars="present", var_name="model", value_name="probability")) pd.DataFrame({"stations": [len(survey)], "share present": [present.mean()]}) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | stations | share present | |-----------:|----------------:| | 800 | 0.775 | ::: ::: ::: The species was caught at 78% of the 800 stations, so presence is the common answer here. yardstick treats the first level of the outcome as the event a measure is about, and `present` lists `yes` first, so every measure below is about presence. In scikit-learn the outcome is `True` for presence, which its measures take as the event by default. ### At 0.5, both models call nearly every station present At the default threshold of 0.5, predicting the share present calls every station present, since it gives every station a probability near 0.78. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} calls <- predictions |> mutate(called = factor(if_else(probability >= 0.5, "yes", "no"), levels = c("yes", "no"))) at_threshold <- calls |> summarise(accuracy = accuracy_vec(present, called), sensitivity = sensitivity_vec(present, called), specificity = specificity_vec(present, called), precision = precision_vec(present, called), `balanced accuracy` = bal_accuracy_vec(present, called), .by = model) at_threshold |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|model | accuracy| sensitivity| specificity| precision| balanced accuracy| |:----------------------------|--------:|-----------:|-----------:|---------:|-----------------:| |Predicting the share present | 0.775| 1.000| 0.000| 0.775| 0.500| |Logistic regression | 0.782| 0.989| 0.072| 0.786| 0.530| |Random forest | 0.785| 0.950| 0.217| 0.807| 0.583|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} def at_threshold(g, threshold=0.5): called = g.probability >= threshold return pd.Series({ "accuracy": accuracy_score(g.present, called), "sensitivity": recall_score(g.present, called), # specificity is the sensitivity for absence "specificity": recall_score(g.present, called, pos_label=False), "precision": precision_score(g.present, called), "balanced accuracy": balanced_accuracy_score(g.present, called), }) calls = (predictions.groupby("model", sort=False) .apply(at_threshold, include_groups=False).reset_index()) calls.round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | model | accuracy | sensitivity | specificity | precision | balanced accuracy | |:-----------------------------|-----------:|--------------:|--------------:|------------:|--------------------:| | Predicting the share present | 0.775 | 1 | 0 | 0.775 | 0.5 | | Logistic regression | 0.778 | 0.984 | 0.067 | 0.784 | 0.525 | | Random forest | 0.784 | 0.945 | 0.228 | 0.808 | 0.586 | ::: ::: ::: The rule finds every presence, so its sensitivity is 1, and calls every absence wrong, so its specificity is 0. Its accuracy, 78%, is just the share of stations with the species. The two models are not far from it. Both have a sensitivity near 1, and of the 180 stations without the species, logistic regression called only 13 absent and the random forest 39. Their accuracy is no better than the rule's: 78% for logistic regression and 78% for the forest. Precision moves little too, since with presence this common most calls of present are right whatever the model. Balanced accuracy shows the difference more clearly: 0.500 for the rule, 0.530 for logistic regression and 0.583 for the forest. Both models are only a little better than the rule at this threshold, and the forest is the better of the two. ### The forest ranks the stations better than logistic regression Predicting the share present is left out here. Within a fold it gives every station the same probability, so it ranks nothing. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ranked <- filter(predictions, model != rule) |> mutate(model = fct_drop(model)) ranked |> summarise(`ROC AUC` = round(roc_auc_vec(present, probability), 3), .by = model) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|model | ROC AUC| |:-------------------|-------:| |Logistic regression | 0.671| |Random forest | 0.723|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} ranked = predictions[predictions["model"] != "Predicting the share present"] (ranked.groupby("model", sort=False) .apply(lambda g: pd.Series({"ROC AUC": roc_auc_score(g.present, g.probability)}), include_groups=False) .reset_index().round(3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | model | ROC AUC | |:--------------------|----------:| | Logistic regression | 0.65 | | Random forest | 0.703 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(curves, aes(specificity, sensitivity, colour = model)) + geom_abline(intercept = 1, slope = 1, colour = "grey70", linetype = "dashed") + geom_path(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(data = default_calls, size = 3.2) + scale_x_reverse() + scale_colour_ml() + coord_equal() + labs(x = "Specificity", y = "Sensitivity", colour = NULL) + theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![ROC curves of the two models' out-of-fold probabilities, showing sensitivity against specificity at every threshold. The dashed diagonal is ranking at random. The points mark the default threshold of 0.5, high on sensitivity and low on specificity. The forest's curve, with a ROC AUC of 0.723, lies above logistic regression's, at 0.671.](classification-metrics_files/figure-html/fig-roc-1.png){#fig-roc fig-alt='A plot of sensitivity from 0 to 1 against specificity running from 1 on the left to 0 on the right, with a dashed diagonal from the bottom left to the top right. Two curves rise from the bottom left corner to the top right corner, both above the diagonal. The orange curve, the random forest, lies above the blue one, logistic regression, along most of its length. A point on each curve marks the threshold of 0.5, both near the top right corner, logistic regression at specificity 0.07 and the forest at 0.22.' width=1120} ::: ::: ::: The forest's ROC AUC is 0.723, and logistic regression's 0.671: in about 72 of 100 pairs of a station with the species and one without, the forest gives the station with the species the higher probability. Its curve lies above the other along most of its length, so whatever threshold is chosen, the forest can reach the same sensitivity with fewer false alarms. The points show why the first part made the two models look so alike: 0.5 sits near the top right corner, where the curves are closest. ### Both models' probabilities can be read as chances The calibration plot sorts each model's stations by their predicted probability into eight groups of 100, and plots each group's average probability against the share of its stations where the species was caught. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(calibration, aes(predicted, observed, colour = model)) + geom_abline(colour = "grey70", linetype = "dashed") + geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 2.8) + annotate("point", x = share_present, y = share_present, shape = 4, size = 5, stroke = 1.6, colour = "grey45") + scale_colour_ml() + coord_equal(xlim = c(0.3, 1), ylim = c(0.3, 1)) + labs(x = "Average predicted probability", y = "Share with the species", colour = NULL) + theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Calibration of the two models' out-of-fold probabilities, in eight groups of 100 stations each. Points on the dashed diagonal mean the probabilities can be read as chances. The grey cross is predicting the share present, which gives every station the same probability. Both models stay close to the diagonal; the forest's groups spread from 0.40 to 0.96, wider than logistic regression's.](classification-metrics_files/figure-html/fig-calibration-1.png){#fig-calibration fig-alt='A plot of the share of stations with the species against the average predicted probability, both from 0.3 to 1, with a dashed diagonal. Eight blue points for logistic regression run from 0.54 to 0.93 along the diagonal, a little above or below it. Eight orange points for the random forest run further, from 0.40 to 0.96, also close to the diagonal. A single grey cross for predicting the share present sits on the diagonal at 0.78.' width=1120} ::: ::: ::: Both models' groups stay close to the diagonal, so their probabilities can be read as chances. Predicting the share present is calibrated too: it says 0.78 everywhere, and the species was caught at 78% of the stations. What it lacks is spread. The forest's groups run from 0.40 to 0.96, wider than logistic regression's, and that spread is what gave it the higher ROC AUC. The measure to report follows from how the predictions will be used, which [Choosing measures that match the objective](choosing-a-metric.qmd) sets out. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - Presence can be scored on the **calls** at one threshold, on the **ranking** the probabilities make, or on whether the probabilities are **calibrated**. A model can look much the same on one and clearly better on another. - **Sensitivity**, **specificity** and **precision** count misses and false alarms apart. **Balanced accuracy**, the average of sensitivity and specificity, scores a rule that calls every station present at 0.5. - **ROC AUC** is the area under the curve of sensitivity against specificity: the share of pairs, one station with the species and one without, ranked the right way round. It is 0.5 for ranking at random, and it ignores how high or low the probabilities are. - A **calibration plot** shows whether a predicted 0.8 means 8 in 10. - yardstick treats the first level of the outcome as the event. Check the levels before trusting any of these measures. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Add a fourth model: logistic regression with `step_upsample(present)` from the `themis` package at the end of its recipe, as in [Class imbalance](../06-assumptions-limitations/class-imbalance.qmd). Predict first: does its ROC AUC move, and does its calibration plot stay on the diagonal? 2. Score the three models on `rare_species` instead of `present`. How do the accuracy and the balanced accuracy of predicting the share present change when the species is rare?
